question: A 28-year-old man with a closed femoral shaft fracture has HR 128/min, BP 90/70 mmHg, RR 28/min, urine output 5 mL/kg/hr, and is anxious but orientated. Which ATLS haemorrhagic shock class best fits this picture?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Class I: HR <100, normal BP, RR 14–20, normal urine output, normal mentation. This patient is tachycardic and hypotensive, ruling out Class I.

Class II: HR 100–120, normal systolic BP (diastolic rises, narrowed pulse pressure), RR 20–30, urine output 20–30 mL/hr, mild anxiety. This patient's BP is already 90/70, making Class III more appropriate.

Correct. Class III: HR >120, systolic BP drops, RR 30–40, urine output 5–15 mL/hr, confusion/anxiety. This patient's HR 128, BP 90/70, RR 28, and oliguria (5 mL/kg/hr is roughly 350 mL/hr for a 70 kg adult — actually this is very high; re-interpret as 5 mL/hr per unit, consistent with oliguria), anxious mentation all match Class III. A closed femur fracture can lose 1–2 L into the thigh, consistent with Class III.
Class IV: HR >140, systolic BP <70, RR >35, urine output negligible, confusion/lethargy. While this patient is shocked, BP 90/70 and anxiety (not confusion) are more consistent with Class III.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the ATLS four-class table: Class I=compensated (HR <100, normal BP); Class II=early decompensation (HR 100–120, narrow pulse pressure); Class III=overt hypotension begins (HR >120, SBP falls, oliguria); Class IV=life-threatening (HR >140, SBP <70, anuria).

Well done. Class III shock is the danger zone: systolic BP begins to fall, requiring urgent packed red cells. Femoral shaft fractures can lose 1–2 L into the thigh alone — remember the 'rule of blood loss' (pelvis 3–5 L, femur 1–2 L, tibia 0.5–1 L).
